title: Dido hospita. Aeneas se aperit
titleEn: Dido's Welcome; Aeneas Steps from the Cloud — Aeneid I.561–656
part: Dido's Welcome; Aeneas Steps from the Cloud (I.561–656)
about: Dido answers Ilioneus briefly, with lowered face. She tells the Trojans to lay aside fear: a hard necessity and a kingdom still new force her to post guards along her whole frontier, but who does not know the race of Aeneas and the story of Troy? The Carthaginians are not dull of heart, and the Sun does not yoke his horses so far from their city. Whether the Trojans want Italy or Sicily and King Acestes, she will send them off safe and help them; or they may settle with her, and Trojan and Tyrian will be treated alike. She wishes Aeneas himself had been driven here by the same wind, and promises to send men along the coast and through Libya to search for him. Achates and Aeneas, who have been burning to break out of their cloud, hear these words; Achates asks what Aeneas now intends, since the ships and men are safe, all but one who was drowned before their eyes, and everything else agrees with his mother's word. Hardly has he spoken when the cloud splits and melts away into clear air. Aeneas stands revealed in bright light, like a god in face and shoulders, for his mother has breathed beauty on his hair and a youthful glow on his eyes, as an artist's hand adds grace to ivory or gold is set about silver or Parian marble. He speaks to the queen and to all: here is the man you seek. He cannot repay her, who alone pities the leavings of Troy and takes them into her city and home; he prays that the gods repay her, and promises that while rivers run, shadows move and heaven feeds the stars, her honour and name will last in every land he is called to. He clasps the hands of Ilioneus, Serestus, Gyas and Cloanthus. Dido is stunned, first by his look and then by his fall, and answers: what chance drives him on, is he truly the Aeneas whom Venus bore to Anchises by the Simois? She remembers Teucer coming to Sidon, and since then she has known the fate of Troy and the names of its kings. She invites the Trojans in; she too has been long hunted by fortune and has learnt to help the wretched. She leads Aeneas to the palace, orders sacrifice at the temples, and sends supplies to the ships. The palace is made ready for a feast, with purple hangings, silver and the ancestral deeds engraved in gold. Aeneas sends Achates to fetch Ascanius, with gifts rescued from Troy: Helen's embroidered robe and veil, Ilione's sceptre, a pearl necklace and a double crown. Achates hurries to the ships.

sentences.t: Tum breviter Dido, voltum demissa, profatur:
sentences.l: Then briefly Dido, her face cast down, speaks forth:
sentences.i: Then Dido, her face lowered, answers briefly:
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and Dido's first speech (562–578). 'voltum demissa' — 'lowered as to her face': a perfect passive participle with an accusative of respect, a Greek-style construction you will see constantly in Virgil. Greenough prints 'voltum' for 'vultum'. 'profatur' — historical present of the deponent 'profor'; the colon leads into the speech.

sentences.t: “Solvite corde metum, Teucri, secludite curas.
sentences.l: “Loosen from the heart your fear, Trojans, shut away your cares.
sentences.i: “Let the fear go from your hearts, Trojans, and put your troubles away.
sentences.n: 'corde' — ablative of separation (no preposition), singular because 'the heart' is each man's own. 'Teucri' — vocative plural. Two imperatives, 'solvite' and 'secludite'; the second is literally 'shut away, shut out'.

sentences.t:
Res dura et regni novitas me talia cogunt
moliri, et late finis custode tueri.
sentences.l:
A hard situation and the newness of the kingdom force me
to attempt such things, and to guard the frontiers widely with a sentry.
sentences.i: The harshness of my position and the youth of my kingdom oblige me to such measures, and to watch my borders far and wide with a guard.
sentences.n: 'Res dura et regni novitas' are the double subject of 'cogunt' (plural verb). 'me… moliri… tueri' — 'cogunt' takes an accusative and infinitive: 'force me to undertake, and to protect'. 'moliri' is deponent. 'finis' — accusative plural in -is, for 'fines'. 'custode' — ablative of means, singular for collective: 'with a guard'. 'late' — 'widely'. Dido explains why her coast guards turned the Trojans back (Ilioneus's complaint, 539–541).

sentences.t:
Quis genus Aeneadum, quis Troiae nesciat urbem,
virtutesque virosque, aut tanti incendia belli?
sentences.l:
Who would not know the race of the Aeneadae, who the city of Troy,
and its valours and its men, or the fires of so great a war?
sentences.i: Who is there that would not know the line of Aeneas, who the city of Troy, its heroism and its heroes, or the burning of a war so great?
sentences.n: 'Quis… nesciat' — a rhetorical question with the potential subjunctive: 'who would be ignorant?', i.e. nobody. 'quis' stands for 'quis' as a plain interrogative pronoun (nominative). 'Aeneadum' — the old genitive plural in -um. 'virtutesque virosque' — 'both valours and men', with the double -que you will see constantly. 'tanti… belli' — genitive of 'tantum bellum', 'so great a war'.

sentences.t:
Non obtusa adeo gestamus pectora Poeni,
nec tam aversus equos Tyria Sol iungit ab urbe.
sentences.l:
We Phoenicians do not carry hearts so blunted,
nor does the Sun yoke his horses so far turned from the Tyrian city.
sentences.i: We Carthaginians do not carry hearts so dull, and the Sun does not drive his team so far from our Tyrian city.
sentences.n: 'Poeni' — the Phoenicians, whose descendants the Carthaginians were (hence 'Punic'). 'obtusa… pectora' — 'blunted hearts': a figure from a dulled blade. 'gestamus' — 'we bear about'. 'aversus' — 'turned away', nominative with 'Sol', predicative: the Sun does not yoke 'turned away'. 'equos' — accusative plural. The sense: we are not at the world's remote edge, outside the news of the age.

sentences.t:
Seu vos Hesperiam magnam Saturniaque arva,
sive Erycis finis regemque optatis Acesten,
auxilio tutos dimittam, opibusque iuvabo.
sentences.l:
Whether you want great Hesperia and the Saturnian fields,
or the borders of Eryx and King Acestes,
I will send you off made safe with an escort, and help you with my means.
sentences.i: Whether you are making for great Hesperia and the lands of Saturn, or for the borders of Eryx and King Acestes, I shall see you off safe with an escort and help you from my resources.
sentences.n: 'Seu… sive… optatis' — 'whether… or…': the single verb 'optatis' (you wish for) comes at the end and serves both halves. 'Hesperiam' — 'the western land', Italy; 'Saturnia arva' — the fields of Saturn, who in legend had ruled in Italy. 'Erycis finis' — 'the borders of Eryx' (the mountain in western Sicily); 'finis' is accusative plural. 'auxilio' — ablative of means, here 'with an escort or aid'; 'tutos' is predicative, 'as safe men'.

sentences.t: Voltis et his mecum pariter considere regnis;
sentences.l: Or do you wish to settle with me here equally in these realms;
sentences.i: Or if you wish instead to settle here with me, as equals, in this realm:
sentences.n: 'Voltis' — Greenough's spelling of 'vultis'. 'considere' is the infinitive of 'consido', 'to settle down'. 'his… regnis' — ablative of place without a preposition. 'pariter' — 'equally, on equal terms'. The semicolon links to what follows.

sentences.t: urbem quam statuo vestra est, subducite navis;
sentences.l: the city which I found is yours; draw up the ships;
sentences.i: the city I am founding is yours; haul your ships ashore;
sentences.n: 'urbem quam statuo vestra est' — the antecedent has been drawn into the relative clause ('the city which I found is yours'); it is a common Latin arrangement. 'statuo' — 'I set up, found'. 'subducite navis' — 'draw up (on the beach)': 'navis' is accusative plural in -is.

sentences.t: Tros Tyriusque mihi nullo discrimine agetur.
sentences.l: Trojan and Tyrian will be handled by me with no distinction.
sentences.i: Trojan and Tyrian will be one to me, with no difference between them.
sentences.n: 'Tros Tyriusque' — 'both Trojan and Tyrian', singular nouns for the two peoples. 'agetur' — future passive of 'ago' in a sense like 'will be dealt with, treated'. 'nullo discrimine' — ablative of manner, 'with no distinction'. 'mihi' is a dative of the agent with a passive verb (here almost 'by me').

sentences.t:
Atque utinam rex ipse Noto compulsus eodem
adforet Aeneas!
sentences.l:
And would that the king himself, driven by the same South wind,
were present, Aeneas!
sentences.i: And if only the king himself, driven by the same south wind, were here — Aeneas!
sentences.n: 'Atque utinam… adforet' — 'utinam' with the imperfect subjunctive expresses a wish about the present that cannot be fulfilled as things stand. 'adforet' is an old form of 'adesset' (the 'fore' forms, as 'forem' for 'essem'). 'Noto… eodem' — the same wind (Notus, the South wind) that drove the Trojans; 'compulsus' agrees with 'Aeneas'. The exclamation puts the name at the end.

sentences.t:
Equidem per litora certos
dimittam et Libyae lustrare extrema iubebo,
si quibus eiectus silvis aut urbibus errat.”
sentences.l:
Indeed I will send out reliable men along the shores, and I shall order them to search
the far parts of Libya,
if he is wandering, cast out in any forests or cities.”
sentences.i: Truly, I shall send trusty men along the coast and bid them search the farthest reaches of Libya, in case he is wandering cast ashore in some woodland or town.”
sentences.n: 'Equidem' — 'for my part, indeed', usually with a first-person verb. 'dimittam' — 'I will send off'; 'iubebo' takes an infinitive, 'lustrare', whose subject is the men just sent (understood). 'extrema' is a neuter plural noun, 'the far parts'. 'si quibus… silvis aut urbibus' — 'if in any woods or cities' (after 'si', 'quibus' means 'any'). 'eiectus' — 'thrown out' by the sea. The closing mark ends Dido's speech.

sentences.t:
His animum arrecti dictis et fortis Achates
et pater Aeneas iamdudum erumpere nubem
ardebant.
sentences.l:
Roused in spirit by these words, both brave Achates
and father Aeneas had been burning for some time
to burst out of the cloud.
sentences.i: Heartened by these words, brave Achates and father Aeneas had both been longing for some time to burst out of the cloud.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'His animum arrecti dictis' — 'aroused as to their spirit by these words': 'animum' is the accusative of respect again, 'dictis' ablative of cause. 'arrecti' agrees with both subjects. 'iamdudum' with the imperfect 'ardebant' — 'had been burning for a long time already'. 'erumpere nubem' — the infinitive with an accusative object, 'to break out of (burst through) the cloud'. The cloud is the mist Venus put round them at I.411 ff. 'pater' is Aeneas's title as father of his people.

sentences.t: Prior Aenean compellat Achates:
sentences.l: First Achates addresses Aeneas:
sentences.i: Achates is first to speak to Aeneas:
sentences.n: 'Prior' — an adjective used as an adverb, 'first'. 'Aenean' — Greek accusative. 'compellat' — 'addresses'. The colon opens Achates's short speech.

sentences.t: “Nate dea, quae nunc animo sententia surgit?
sentences.l: “Goddess-born, what resolve now rises in your mind?
sentences.i: “Son of a goddess, what is your purpose now that it rises in your mind?
sentences.n: 'Nate dea' — vocative 'nate', with 'dea' ablative of origin: 'born from a goddess'. 'animo' — either dative or ablative; 'surgit' — 'rises up'. 'quae sententia' — 'what purpose'.

sentences.t: omnia tuta vides, classem sociosque receptos.
sentences.l: You see everything safe: the fleet and companions recovered.
sentences.i: You see everything safe, the fleet and our friends recovered.
sentences.n: 'omnia tuta vides' — 'tuta' is predicative with 'omnia'. 'receptos' — the participle agrees with 'sociosque' (the nearer noun), but belongs to 'classem' too. Achates is pointing to Ilioneus's embassy: the lost ships have been found.

sentences.t:
Unus abest, medio in fluctu quem vidimus ipsi
submersum;
sentences.l:
One is missing, whom in the middle of the wave we ourselves
saw sunk;
sentences.i: One alone is missing, whom we ourselves watched go under in the midst of the waves;
sentences.n: 'Unus abest' — the missing man is Orontes, whose ship was swallowed by the sea at I.113–117. 'quem vidimus ipsi submersum' — 'whom we saw (as) sunk': the participle is predicative. 'ipsi' — 'we ourselves', so there can be no doubt.

sentences.t: dictis respondent cetera matris.”
sentences.l: the rest of what your mother said agrees.”
sentences.i: all else bears out your mother's words.”
sentences.n: 'dictis respondent cetera matris' — 'the other things answer to the words of your mother'; 'cetera' is neuter plural, the subject of the plural verb. 'respondent' means 'correspond, tally with'. The words are Venus's prophecy at I.390 ff. that his lost ships would be safe. The closing mark ends Achates's speech.

sentences.t:
Vix ea fatus erat, cum circumfusa repente
scindit se nubes et in aethera purgat apertum.
sentences.l:
Scarcely had he said these things, when the surrounding cloud
splits itself suddenly and clears away into the open air.
sentences.i: Scarcely had he spoken when the cloud about them parted all at once, and melted away into the open sky.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Vix ea fatus erat, cum' — 'scarcely had he said these things when': the 'cum' clause carries the main event, so it takes the indicative. 'fatus erat' — pluperfect of the deponent 'for'. 'scindit se' — a reflexive where English would say 'is torn apart'; 'circumfusa' — 'poured around'. 'in aethera purgat apertum' — 'clears into the open air'; 'purgat' is used intransitively, with the cloud as subject.

sentences.t:
Restitit Aeneas claraque in luce refulsit,
os umerosque deo similis;
sentences.l:
Aeneas stood and shone out in the clear light,
like a god in face and shoulders;
sentences.i: Aeneas stood still and shone out in the bright light, like a god in face and shoulders;
sentences.n: 'Restitit… refulsit' — two perfects: he stopped, and shone. 'os umerosque deo similis' — accusative of respect with 'similis': 'like a god as to face and shoulders', and 'deo' is the dative after 'similis'. 'clara in luce' — in the clear daylight, now that the cloud is gone.

sentences.t:
namque ipsa decoram
caesariem nato genetrix lumenque iuventae
purpureum et laetos oculis adflarat honores:
sentences.l:
for his mother herself had breathed on her son handsome
hair and the purple glow of youth
and glad grace on his eyes:
sentences.i: for his mother herself had breathed upon her son a noble head of hair, the bright bloom of youth, and a joyous charm in his eyes:
sentences.n: 'namque' explains the god-like look. 'adflarat' is the contracted form of 'adflaverat', pluperfect; 'ipsa genetrix' is Venus. 'purpureum' is used of light and brightness, not just colour (a 'shining' youth). 'oculis' is dative of the person affected; 'laetos honores' — 'glad adornments', that is grace. The colon leads into a comparison.

sentences.t:
quale manus addunt ebori decus, aut ubi flavo
argentum Pariusve lapis circumdatur auro.
sentences.l:
as hands add beauty to ivory, or when silver
or Parian stone is set around with yellow gold.
sentences.i: as when craftsmen's hands lend ivory its beauty, or when silver, or marble from Paros, is set round with yellow gold.
sentences.n: A short simile with 'quale' standing without its correlative 'tale'. 'manus' — 'hands' for the craftsman's skill. 'ubi' with the present: 'or when'. 'Pariusve lapis' — the marble of the island of Paros. 'circumdatur' is the passive: the metal is set around the other.

sentences.t:
Tum sic reginam adloquitur, cunctisque repente
improvisus ait:
sentences.l:
Then thus he addresses the queen, and to all
unforeseen he says:
sentences.i: Then he speaks to the queen thus, and, unlooked-for by all, says:
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and Aeneas's speech (595–610). 'adloquitur' is a historical present, deponent. 'improvisus' — 'unforeseen' (as the one who appears), predicative, with 'cunctis' dative. 'repente' — suddenly. The colon introduces the speech.

sentences.t:
“Coram, quem quaeritis, adsum,
Troius Aeneas, Lybicis ereptus ab undis.
sentences.l:
“Here, whom you seek, I am present,
Trojan Aeneas, snatched from the Libyan waves.
sentences.i: “Here I am, the man you are looking for, Aeneas of Troy, rescued from the Libyan waves.
sentences.n: 'Coram' — 'in person, face to face'. The relative clause 'quem quaeritis' comes before its unexpressed antecedent; the sentence is 'I am here, whom you seek'. 'Troius' is the adjective ('Trojan'). Greenough prints 'Lybicis'; the Latin Library prints 'Libycis' — the same word. 'ereptus' — 'snatched away', hence 'rescued'.

sentences.t:
O sola infandos Troiae miserata labores,
quae nos, reliquias Danaum, terraeque marisque
omnibus exhaustos iam casibus, omnium egenos,
urbe, domo, socias,
sentences.l:
O you alone who pitied the unspeakable labours of Troy,
you who us, the remnant of the Danaans, worn out
by all the misfortunes of land and sea, in want of everything,
associate with your city, your home,
sentences.i: You alone have taken pity on the terrible labours of Troy; you take us in, the remnant left by the Greeks, worn out by every misfortune of land and sea and short of everything, to share your city and your home.
sentences.n: The long period is built on a vocative: 'O sola… miserata' (the participle of the deponent 'miseror', 'pity', agreeing with 'sola'). 'infandos' — 'unspeakable'. 'quae nos… socias' — 'you who associate us…': 'socias' is the second singular of 'socio', and its objects, 'nos reliquias Danaum', are glossed by two participial phrases. 'reliquias Danaum' — 'the remnant of the Danaans' (old genitive plural -um), the Greeks who had left them alive. 'terraeque marisque' — genitive of 'terra' and 'mare', both with 'casibus'. 'omnium egenos' — 'in need of all things', the adjective with a genitive. 'urbe, domo' — ablatives, 'in your city, your home'.

sentences.t:
grates persolvere dignas
non opis est nostrae, Dido, nec quicquid ubique est
gentis Dardaniae, magnum quae sparsa per orbem.
sentences.l:
to pay back worthy thanks is not within our means, Dido,
nor of whatever there is anywhere
of the Dardan nation, which is scattered across the great world.
sentences.i: To repay you as you deserve is beyond our power, Dido, and beyond that of all that remains anywhere of the Trojan race, scattered over the wide world.
sentences.n: 'grates persolvere dignas non opis est nostrae' — the infinitive phrase is the subject; 'opis nostrae' is a predicate genitive, 'it is not of our power'. 'grates' is the archaic accusative plural of 'gratia' (thanks, found only in this plural). 'nec quicquid ubique est gentis Dardaniae' — 'nor [is it of the power of] whatever there is anywhere of the Dardan people'. 'quae sparsa' — 'which is scattered', with 'quae' referring to the people.

sentences.t:
Di tibi, si qua pios respectant numina, si quid
usquam iustitia est et mens sibi conscia recti,
praemia digna ferant.
sentences.l:
May the gods bring you worthy rewards, if any divine powers
look upon the dutiful, if anywhere there is anything of justice
and a mind aware to itself of what is right.
sentences.i: May the gods give you the rewards you deserve — if any divine powers watch over the dutiful, if justice is anywhere a living thing, and a mind that knows itself upright.
sentences.n: 'Di tibi… praemia digna ferant' — a jussive (wishing) subjunctive, 'may they bring'. 'Di' is the contracted nominative plural of 'deus'. 'si qua… numina respectant' and 'si quid… iustitia est' — two conditions, offered as hope; 'pios' means those who do their duty to gods, kin and guests. 'mens sibi conscia recti' — 'a mind conscious to itself of the right', the genitive 'recti' with 'conscia'.

sentences.t:
Quae te tam laeta tulerunt
saecula?
sentences.l:
What so happy
ages bore you?
sentences.i:
What age, so happy,
gave you birth?
sentences.n: 'Quae… saecula' — 'saecula' is the neuter plural, 'what ages', so 'tulerunt' is plural. The question is exclamatory and rhetorical, praise in the form of astonishment. 'te tulerunt' — 'bore you'.

sentences.t: Qui tanti talem genuere parentes?
sentences.l: What parents of such stature begot such a one?
sentences.i: What parents, so great, brought forth a woman like you?
sentences.n: 'Qui tanti talem genuere parentes' — 'genuere' is the third plural perfect '-ere' for '-erunt', which you will see constantly. 'tanti' agrees with 'parentes', 'talem' is the object: 'such parents, such a daughter'.

sentences.t:
In freta dum fluvii current, dum montibus umbrae
lustrabunt convexa, polus dum sidera pascet,
semper honos nomenque tuum laudesque manebunt,
quae me cumque vocant terrae.
sentences.l:
As long as rivers run into the seas, as long as shadows
will range over the hollows of the mountains, as long as heaven feeds the stars,
always your honour and name and praises will remain,
whatever lands call me.”
sentences.i: As long as rivers run down to the sea, as long as shadows roam the mountain slopes, as long as the heavens feed the stars, your honour, your name and your praises will remain with me, whatever lands may call me.”
sentences.n: A vow of everlasting memory in a series of 'dum' clauses; 'dum' with the future ('current', 'lustrabunt', 'pascet') means 'so long as'. 'polus' — the vault of heaven. 'convexa' — neuter plural, 'the hollows' or 'slopes'. The main clause comes after: the plural verb 'manebunt' agrees with three subjects ('honos nomenque tuum laudesque'). 'quae me cumque vocant terrae' is a tmesis, the splitting of the word 'quaecumque' by the insertion of 'me': 'whatever lands call me'.

sentences.t:
”Sic fatus, amicum
Ilionea petit dextra, laevaque Serestum,
post alios, fortemque Gyan fortemque Cloanthum.
sentences.l:
Having thus spoken, he seeks his friend
Ilioneus with his right hand, and Serestus with his left,
after the others, brave Gyas and brave Cloanthus.
sentences.i: Having spoken so, he takes his friend Ilioneus by the right hand and Serestus by the left, then the others, brave Gyas and brave Cloanthus.
sentences.n: The closing speech mark of Aeneas is printed in Greenough's text after a space and glued to 'Sic' ('terrae. ”Sic'), so the mark heads this unit's `t`; it is carried in the `l` and `i` of the previous unit, where the speech ends. 'Sic fatus' — 'having thus spoken', the perfect participle of the deponent 'for'. 'petit' — 'seeks', here 'reaches for'. 'Ilionea… Gyan' — Greek accusatives. 'dextra… laevaque' — ablatives of means. 'fortem… fortemque' — the double -que once more.

sentences.t:
Obstipuit primo aspectu Sidonia Dido,
casu deinde viri tanto, et sic ore locuta est:
sentences.l:
Sidonian Dido was stunned at first sight,
then at the heavy fortune of the man, and thus with her mouth spoke:
sentences.i: Sidonian Dido was struck dumb, first by the sight of him, then by the great misfortune of the man, and she spoke thus:
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Obstipuit' — perfect of 'obstipesco', 'was stunned'. 'primo aspectu' — ablative of cause; 'casu… tanto' likewise. 'Sidonia' — 'of Sidon', a Phoenician city, so 'Phoenician'. 'locuta est' — perfect of the deponent 'loquor'; the colon opens Dido's second speech (615–630).

sentences.t:
“Quis te, nate dea, per tanta pericula casus
insequitur?
sentences.l:
“What chance, goddess-born, through such perils
pursues you?
sentences.i: “What fortune, son of a goddess, hounds you through such dangers?
sentences.n: 'Quis… casus' — 'quis' for 'qui', as an adjective with 'casus'. 'nate dea' — the same vocative as Achates used at 582. 'insequitur' — the compound verb, 'pursues'.

sentences.t: Quae vis immanibus applicat oris?
sentences.l: What force brings you to savage shores?
sentences.i: What power drives you ashore on this wild coast?
sentences.n: 'applicat' — 'puts you in, drives you up to'; 'immanibus… oris' is dative, 'savage' (strictly: monstrous, beyond measure). It is an expression that brings in the Libyan coast as Dido sees it from the outside, a land she herself has made a city in.

sentences.t:
Tune ille Aeneas, quem Dardanio Anchisae
alma Venus Phrygii genuit Simoentis ad undam?
sentences.l:
Are you that Aeneas, whom to Dardanian Anchises
nurturing Venus bore by the wave of Phrygian Simois?
sentences.i: Can you be that Aeneas whom kindly Venus bore to Anchises of Dardanus's line, beside the waters of the Phrygian Simois?
sentences.n: 'Tune' — 'tu' + enclitic '-ne' (a yes-or-no question). 'ille Aeneas' — 'that famous Aeneas'. 'Dardanio Anchisae' — dative of the father: 'bore to Anchises' (a Dardanian, that is a Trojan, by descent). 'alma Venus' — 'nourishing Venus', a standing epithet. 'Simoentis' is the Greek genitive of Simois, the Trojan river.

sentences.i: And in truth I remember that Teucer came to Sidon, driven from his homeland, seeking a new kingdom with the help of Belus;
sentences.n: 'memini' takes an accusative and infinitive: 'I remember Teucer (to) come'. This is the Greek Teucer, son of Telamon, exiled by his father, who is said to have founded Salamis in Cyprus. 'Sidona' — Greek accusative. 'finibus… patriis' — ablative of separation, 'from his native borders'. 'auxilio Beli' — 'with the help of Belus', ablative of means; Belus is Dido's father.

sentences.t:
genitor tum Belus opimam
vastabat Cyprum, et victor dicione tenebat.
sentences.l:
my father Belus was then laying waste rich Cyprus,
and as victor held it in his power.
sentences.i: my father Belus was then ravaging wealthy Cyprus, and held it, victorious, under his rule.
sentences.n: 'genitor tum Belus' — Dido speaks of her own father. 'vastabat… tenebat' — two imperfects. 'dicione' — ablative, 'under his sway'. 'victor' is a noun used as an adjective (predicative), 'as victor'.

sentences.t:
Tempore iam ex illo casus mihi cognitus urbis
Troianae nomenque tuum regesque Pelasgi.
sentences.l:
From that time already the fate of the Trojan city was known to me,
and your name, and the Pelasgian kings.
sentences.i: From that time on I have known the fall of the Trojan city, and your name, and the Greek kings.
sentences.n: 'Tempore iam ex illo' — 'from that time already'. 'casus' is the subject with 'nomen' and 'reges'; 'cognitus' agrees with the nearest word (as in 583 above). 'est' is understood. 'mihi' is a dative of the agent. 'Pelasgi' — the Pelasgians are an old name for the Greeks.

sentences.t:
Ipse hostis Teucros insigni laude ferebat,
seque ortum antiqua Teucrorum ab stirpe volebat.
sentences.l:
He himself, an enemy, used to raise the Teucrians with distinguished praise,
and wanted himself to be believed sprung from the ancient stock of the Teucrians.
sentences.i: He himself, though their enemy, used to lift the Trojans high with conspicuous praise, and claimed that he came from the old stock of the Teucrians.
sentences.n: 'Ipse hostis' — 'he himself, although an enemy': Belus. 'ferebat' — 'carried up, extolled'. 'seque ortum… volebat' — 'se' is the subject of an understood infinitive 'esse': 'he wanted (it) that he himself was sprung', that is, he wished to be thought a descendant. Teucer was a Trojan on his mother's side (his mother, Hesione, was a daughter of Laomedon). 'Teucrorum' — old genitive plural.

sentences.t: Quare agite, O tectis, iuvenes, succedite nostris.
sentences.l: Wherefore come, O young men, step into our dwellings.
sentences.i: So come, young men, and enter beneath our roof.
sentences.n: 'Quare agite' — 'therefore come on' (the imperative of 'ago', used as an exhortation). 'succedite' — 'go up into' with the dative 'tectis nostris'. 'tectis' means 'roofs, houses'.

sentences.t:
Me quoque per multos similis fortuna labores
iactatam hac demum voluit consistere terra.
sentences.l:
Me also a like fortune through many labours
wished to settle, tossed about, in this land at last.
sentences.i: Fortune, which has driven me too through many hardships, has willed that I should at last find rest in this land.
sentences.n: 'Me quoque… iactatam… voluit consistere' — 'voluit' takes the accusative-and-infinitive: 'wished me, tossed about, to settle'. 'similis fortuna' — 'a like fortune', the subject. 'hac demum terra' — 'in this land at last'; 'consistere' — 'to come to rest'.

sentences.t: Non ignara mali, miseris succurrere disco.”
sentences.l: Not ignorant of evil, to come to the aid of the wretched I learn.”
sentences.i: I have known suffering myself, and so I am learning to help the suffering.”
sentences.n: 'Non ignara mali' — 'not ignorant of evil': a litotes (an understatement by negation) with the genitive 'mali' after 'ignara', agreeing with Dido herself. 'miseris succurrere' — dative with the infinitive; 'disco' — 'I learn', a present that suggests a lesson still going on. The closing mark ends Dido's speech.

sentences.t: Sic memorat;
sentences.l: So she speaks;
sentences.i: So she speaks;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Sic memorat' — 'thus she says', the verb of narration after a speech, a historical present. The semicolon joins two simultaneous actions with 'simul… simul'.

sentences.t:
simul Aenean in regia ducit
tecta, simul divom templis indicit honorem.
sentences.l:
at the same time she leads Aeneas into the royal
house, at the same time proclaims honour at the temples of the gods.
sentences.i: at once she leads Aeneas into her royal house, and at once proclaims worship in the temples of the gods.
sentences.n: 'simul… simul' — 'at the same time… at the same time'. 'in regia… tecta' — 'regia' is an adjective, neuter plural, with 'tecta'. 'divom' — old genitive plural of 'deus', with 'templis' (dative: 'to the temples'). 'indicit honorem' — 'proclaims an honour', that is, orders sacrifice.

sentences.t:
Nec minus interea sociis ad litora mittit
viginti tauros, magnorum horrentia centum
terga suum, pinguis centum cum matribus agnos,
munera laetitiamque dii.
sentences.l:
No less meanwhile to the companions on the shore she sends
twenty bulls, the bristling backs of a hundred
great pigs, a hundred fat lambs with their mothers,
gifts and the gladness of the day.
sentences.i: Meanwhile, no less generously, she sends down to her comrades on the shore twenty bulls, a hundred bristling hog-backs, a hundred fat lambs with their ewes: the gifts and the cheer of the feast-day.
sentences.n: 'Nec minus' — 'and none the less'. 'sociis ad litora' — 'to the companions at the shore'. 'terga suum' — 'backs of pigs', the part for the whole (a poetic way of counting animals); 'suum' is the genitive plural of 'sus', 'pig'. 'pinguis… agnos' — accusative plural in -is. 'munera laetitiamque dii' — 'dii' is the old genitive of 'dies': 'the gifts and the gladness of the day'. The line is a half-line, one of the places where Virgil left a verse unfinished: it is metrically incomplete.

sentences.t:
At domus interior regali splendida luxu
instruitur, mediisque parant convivia tectis:
sentences.l:
But the inner house, splendid with royal luxury,
is being fitted out, and in the middle of the palace they prepare a feast:
sentences.i: But within, the palace is being furnished in royal splendour, and in its central halls a banquet is made ready:
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'domus interior' — 'the inner house'. 'regali… luxu' — ablative of quality or means. 'instruitur' — present passive. 'parant' — an indefinite plural, 'they prepare', i.e. the servants. 'mediis tectis' — 'in the midst of the house', ablative of place. The colon introduces a list of the furnishings.

sentences.t:
arte laboratae vestes ostroque superbo,
ingens argentum mensis, caelataque in auro
fortia facta patrum, series longissima rerum
per tot ducta viros antiqua ab origine gentis.
sentences.l:
hangings worked with art, and in proud purple,
huge silver on the tables, and engraved in gold
the brave deeds of the fathers, a very long series of events
drawn through so many men from the ancient origin of the race.
sentences.i: There are hangings wrought with skill and splendid purple, great silver on the tables, and engraved in gold the brave deeds of their ancestors, an endless chain of events running through so many heroes from the ancient beginning of the people.
sentences.n: The list is a set of nominatives with no verb, taken from 'instruitur' above; the construction is loose but clear. 'arte laboratae vestes ostroque superbo' — 'cloths worked with art, and with proud purple' ('ostro' ablative of the dye). 'mensis' — dative or ablative, 'on the tables'. 'caelata… in auro' — 'engraved in gold' (the silver is engraved with scenes). 'series longissima rerum… ducta' — 'a very long chain of events, drawn through so many men'. 'patrum' — 'of the fathers' (ancestors).

sentences.i: Aeneas — for a father's love would not let his mind rest — sends swift Achates on ahead to the ships, to take the news to Ascanius and to bring the boy himself to the city;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. The parenthesis 'neque enim… amor' contains 'passus' with 'est' understood: the perfect of the deponent 'patior', 'allowed'; 'consistere mentem' is accusative and infinitive after it, 'to rest, settle'. 'patrius amor' — an adjective, 'paternal love'. 'rapidum… Achaten' — Greek accusative, 'swift'. 'ferat… ducat' — the subjunctives express purpose or command without 'ut', a common idiom. 'Ascanio' is the dative of the person to whom he carries 'haec'. 'ad moenia' — 'to the walls'.

sentences.t: omnis in Ascanio cari stat cura parentis.
sentences.l: All the care of the dear parent rests in Ascanius.
sentences.i: The whole concern of a loving father stands fixed on Ascanius.
sentences.n: 'omnis… cura' is the subject, 'omnis' is nominative feminine singular. 'in Ascanio stat' — 'rests on Ascanius'. 'cari… parentis' — genitive, 'of the dear father'.

sentences.t:
Munera praeterea, Iliacis erepta ruinis,
ferre iubet, pallam signis auroque rigentem,
et circumtextum croceo velamen acantho,
sentences.l:
Gifts besides, snatched from the ruins of Ilium,
he orders him to bring: a mantle stiff with figures and gold,
and a veil woven round with saffron acanthus,
sentences.i: He also orders him to bring gifts saved from the wreck of Troy: a robe stiff with figures and gold, and a veil bordered all round with yellow acanthus,
sentences.n: 'Munera… erepta' — neuter plural. 'ferre iubet' — 'iubeo' with the infinitive; the subject of 'ferre' (Achates) is understood. 'pallam signis auroque rigentem' — 'stiff with embroidered figures and gold'. 'circumtextum… croceo… acantho' — 'woven round with saffron acanthus': the acanthus is the stylized leaf pattern, in a saffron colour. 'velamen' — 'a covering, veil'.

sentences.t:
ornatus Argivae Helenae, quos illa Mycenis,
Pergama cum peteret inconcessosque hymenaeos,
extulerat, matris Ledae mirabile donum:
sentences.l:
the ornaments of Argive Helen, which she had carried from Mycenae
when she was making for Pergamum and the forbidden marriage,
her mother Leda's marvellous gift:
sentences.i: They were the finery of Argive Helen, which she had brought away from Mycenae when she went to Troy and her unlawful marriage: a wonderful present from her mother Leda:
sentences.n: The gifts are glossed in apposition: 'ornatus Argivae Helenae'. 'Argivae' — 'of Argos', i.e. Greek. 'quos illa… extulerat' — pluperfect, 'she had carried out'. 'Mycenis' — 'from Mycenae' without a preposition; Virgil gives the Greek city, though Helen was Menelaus's wife, from Sparta. 'cum peteret' — imperfect subjunctive with 'cum', temporal-circumstantial. 'inconcessos hymenaeos' — a Greek accusative plural, 'forbidden wedding' (Helen's union with Paris). 'mirabile donum' — apposition.

sentences.t:
praeterea sceptrum, Ilione quod gesserat olim,
maxima natarum Priami, colloque monile
bacatum, et duplicem gemmis auroque coronam.
sentences.l:
Besides, a sceptre, which Ilione had once carried,
the eldest of Priam's daughters, and a necklace for the neck
of pearls, and a double crown of gems and gold.
sentences.i: And also a sceptre that Ilione, Priam's eldest daughter, had once borne; a necklace of pearls for the throat; and a crown, doubled, of gems and gold.
sentences.n: 'Ilione' — a Greek nominative, the eldest daughter of Priam. 'quod gesserat' — 'which she had carried'. 'maxima natarum Priami' — 'greatest of Priam's daughters', that is the eldest; 'natarum' is the genitive plural. 'collo… monile bacatum' — 'a necklace set with berries (pearls)', the adjective from 'bacca'; 'collo' is dative of the person. 'duplicem… coronam' — 'a double crown', a coronet with a second circlet; 'gemmis auroque' are ablatives.

sentences.t: Haec celerans ita ad naves tendebat Achates.
sentences.l: Hurrying these things, thus to the ships Achates was making his way.
sentences.i: With these orders he hurried, and so Achates made his way to the ships.
sentences.n: 'Haec celerans' — 'speeding these things', i.e. carrying out the task quickly. 'ita' — thus, as ordered. 'tendebat' — imperfect, 'was proceeding'.
